analysis.title: Global Economic Weekly: Shaken and stirred
key_insights: BofA argues the equity selloff is not mainly about tech debt issuance. If supply were the worry, long-end US rates would be rising. Instead long-end rates are rallying while equities fall, which BofA reads as doubt that tech firms can monetize their AI investment.

Risk-off drivers this week: the Iran war and Middle East tensions, the AI trade correction, and French 10-year yields at the highest since 2002. French yields are above US 10-year yields for the first time since the Eurozone crisis.

Brent crude is above $110/bbl on expected increased military operations after the US midterm elections. Hostilities hitting refining capacity are also pressuring diesel and other refined products. BofA sees no near-term trigger for de-escalation.

BofA keeps its call for a 25bp Fed hike at the Oct FOMC, but with low conviction, and calls it a heavy lift given this week's price action. Markets price only about a 10% chance of an October hike (2bp priced).

BofA's case for an October hike: Sep inflation beat was large and broad-based enough to offset last month's downward revisions. Core PCE could end 2026 at 3.4% y/y. The 10y yield has nearly fallen back below 5% and term premium is down over 25bp, so the long end is no longer doing the Fed's tightening work.

The Oct decision tests Chair Warsh's resolve to bring a 'sea change' to Fed forward guidance. Williams and Jefferson's forward guidance led markets to price out the October hike, and BofA says it cannot be squared with Warsh's stated objection to forward guidance.

Press conference scenarios: a hike risks an over-tightening 'policy error' trade and a large risk-asset correction with twist-flattening. A hold risks a credibility trade like the July presser: twist steepening, weaker dollar and a moderate risk-asset selloff.
BofA's Fed path is unchanged if the Fed holds in October: two more hikes, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027, with risks of Jun 2027 and perhaps Sep 2027 if y/y inflation stays sticky.

ECB is expected to hold next week with a slightly dovish lean, as tighter financial conditions offset energy-price risks, while keeping a hiking bias. BofA expects one final hike in December, a March hike risk if energy stays high, and cuts in late 2027. Total hiking is 75bp with residual risk of 100bp.

BofA sees room for ECB verbal intervention on long-term rates and spreads, such as a reminder of available tools or a hint that QT could be paused if markets stay disorderly. It sees the bar for stopping or reducing QT as high.

UK Sep CPI rose to 3.5% from 3.1% (0.53% m/m), 10bp above consensus and 44bp above the BoE forecast. Core rose to 2.8% and services to 3.7%. Energy inflation rose to 17.9% and motor fuel prices rose 5.4% m/m.

UK labour data was stronger than expected: unemployment fell to 4.7% from 4.9%, payroll revisions were upward, and private regular pay growth rose to 3.0%. BofA keeps its call for BoE hikes in Nov and Feb to 4.25% and sees market pricing of close to four hikes as excessive.

BofA expects the UK Autumn Budget to be cautious, with pre-measures headroom cut by about £14bn to about £10bn, about £8bn of tax rises by 2029-30, and borrowing of £130.5bn (4.1% of GDP) in FY26-27. A £10bn gross financing top-up is expected to come through net T-bill sales.

Philippines targets a deficit-to-GDP cut from 5.6% in 2025 to 3.5% by 2030E. BofA's Philippine Equity Partners analyst thinks the pace may be slower than shown. The 2027 budget implies a P1.66trn deficit (5.4% of GDP), and the ProGRESS Bill taxes would raise only P40-50bn a year.

Sub-Saharan Africa sentiment is constructive on improving fundamentals and commodities. Investor concern focuses on Kenya and Angola election and fiscal risks and on unresolved Senegal restructuring questions (perimeter, comparability of treatment, LIC-DSF).

Nigeria's CBN cut its policy rate 350bp to 23.0% in September but narrowed the corridor, so BofA estimates effective easing at about 200bp and no longer expects a November cut. South Africa's SARB could hike if domestic inflation surprises up and the Fed hikes.

Oil imports bill has had limited impact on Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic and Guatemala, cushioned by gold and tourism exports, FDI and remittances. Oil is up 31% this year versus the 2025 average.

BofA forecasts: US 10yr 5.00% by Dec-26 (spot 4.96), Brent $100 by Dec-26 (spot 113.6), gold $4,000 by Dec-26 (spot 4043) and $5,000 by mid-2027, S&P 500 target 7100 for end-2027 (spot 7663), EUR/USD 1.15 by Dec-26 (spot 1.12).

sector_views.rationale: BofA says the selloff is led by tech and AI stocks, and markets are questioning whether firms can monetize AI investment. It calls the AI trade breaking possibly the biggest risk to the US outlook.

risk_factors: The AI trade breaking, which BofA calls possibly the biggest risk to the US outlook.
Energy-price shock passing through to core inflation, especially with a booming nominal economy.
Policy-error trades around the October FOMC: over-tightening if the Fed hikes, credibility loss if it holds.
Tight financial conditions and long-end rates and spreads in Europe that could 'break something'.
French fiscal deterioration, with a worse r-g gap than the US.
UK Budget risks: small headroom, backloaded consolidation, large investment spending raising gilt issuance, or changes to fiscal rules.
El Niño as an upside inflation risk in South Africa not in BofA's baseline.
Higher fuel prices weighing on tourism flows in Central America and the Caribbean.

vol_and_positioning: Fed pricing is roughly three more hikes at a quarterly cadence, but only about a 10% chance (2bp) of an October hike.
UK market pricing is close to four BoE hikes, which BofA calls excessive.
BofA says an October Fed hike could cause a large risk-asset correction with twist-flattening if markets price an over-tightening policy mistake.
geopolitical: Iran war and Middle East tensions: reportedly increased military operations after the US midterm elections are keeping crude above $110/bbl, and hostilities are hitting refining capacity.
French social unrest threatens fiscal consolidation ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Re-escalation of the conflict with Iran is expected to push South African inflation above 5% in October.
Kenya and Angola face election and fiscal risks around the August 2027 elections.
Senegal's debt restructuring remains uncertain over perimeter, preferred creditor status and comparability of treatment.
Nigeria's presidential election is on 16 January 2027, with Tinubu the frontrunner.

tension_points.bull_case: BofA argues a hike is warranted: Sep inflation beat was large and broad-based, core PCE could reach 3.4%, and a hike keeps the Dec option and signals Warsh's exit from coordinated messaging.
tension_points.bear_case: Markets price only about 10% odds of a hike. A hike could trigger an over-tightening policy-error trade and a large risk-asset correction, and falling long-end yields signal growth worries about the AI trade.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Something breaking in markets or the AI trade, which BofA says would undercut the case for further hikes.

tension_points.bull_case: The common narrative is that tech debt issuance to fund AI investment is driving the selloff.
tension_points.bear_case: BofA says falling long-end rates alongside falling equities point to doubts about AI monetization and profitability, not debt supply.
tension_points.what_invalidates: US long-end rates climbing higher would support the supply narrative.

theme_stances.key_argument: Long-end rates are rallying while equities sell off, which suggests the market doubts tech firms' ability to monetize AI investment.
theme_stances.evidence: increasingly questioning the ability of tech firms to monetize their investments

theme_stances.key_argument: Inflation is too high and the long end is no longer tightening on the Fed's behalf, so the Fed should hike in October.

theme_stances.key_argument: Inflation above the BoE forecast, sticky underlying services and a stabilizing labour market support a November hike.
theme_stances.evidence: further strengthens the case for our call of an insurance hike
